statement: In people who use drugs in contact with harm-reduction services in North America, using fentanyl test strips compared with not using them: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it changes the risk of overdose. The only study read that compared the two groups followed 732 clients of strip-distributing harm-reduction sites in Kentucky, New York and Ohio for four weeks in 2023: after allowing for state, age, drug use, injecting, earlier overdose and other differences, the modelled risk of a self-reported overdose that people survived (passing out and needing to be revived) was about 2 in 100 days of drug use in both groups (0.02 a day; risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.70 to 2.06, compatible with 30% fewer overdoses or twice as many); before that adjustment it was twice as high in the people who used strips (risk ratio 2.06, 1.09 to 3.89), who more often injected and used fentanyl; deaths could not be counted. A scoping review of 91 studies to March 2023 found only two that reported overdose outcomes, neither with a comparison group: at a supervised injection site most checks came after use (113 of the 120 overdoses recorded followed checks made after use), so its lower odds of overdose among people who said they would use less (crude odds ratio 0.41) cannot show an effect; and after a vending machine began giving out strips with naloxone, county overdose deaths fell by about 10% while the state's rose by about 5%, with no control area. A systematic review of drug checking to 2019 found no other study linking testing with overdose. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In the one study that compared people who used test strips with people who did not, over four weeks, overdoses that people survived were about as common in both groups once other differences were allowed for, but the result is too uncertain to rule out either fewer or more overdoses. Deaths could not be counted. No study read could show whether strips prevent overdoses or deaths.
population: People who use drugs in contact with harm-reduction services in North America: 732 clients of 14 strip-distributing organizations in Kentucky, New York and Ohio (2023); studies in a scoping review (to March 2023) and a systematic review of drug checking services (to October 2019)
exposure: Self-reported use of fentanyl test strips in the 30 days before baseline (cohort); strip checks at a supervised injection site, and a vending machine that dispensed strips (as relayed by the reviews)
comparator: People at the same sites who reported no strip use (cohort); no comparison group in the two studies the scoping review describes
outcome: Self-reported nonfatal overdose over four weeks (cohort); overdoses recorded by nurses with checks, and county overdose deaths and emergency visits (as relayed by the scoping review)
magnitude: Vickers-Smith 2025: mean daily risk 0.02 (0.01–0.03) in both groups; adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70–2.06; n = 677); unadjusted RR 2.06 (1.09–3.89; n = 710); the association was modified by age in adjusted analyses (P = .02). Karamouzian 2018 (card): 113 of 120 overdoses recorded with checks made after use; crude OR 0.41 (0.18–0.89) for intended dose reduction pools checks made before and after use and is not an effect. Kutscher 2024 (relayed): 2 of 91 studies with overdose outcomes; after a vending machine (10,155 strips with naloxone in its first year), county overdose deaths fell about 10% while Ohio's rose about 5%, with no control group.

evidence.locator: Methods › Nonfatal Overdose; Results › Mean Daily Risk of Self-Reported Nonfatal Overdose; Table 3
evidence.extracted: Nonfatal overdose (a time when the participant lost consciousness and someone had to revive them, self-reported on four weekly surveys): unadjusted risk ratio 2.06 (95% CI 1.09–3.89; n = 710) for people who used strips at baseline against those who did not; adjusted 1.20 (0.70–2.06; n = 677), with a mean daily risk of 0.02 (0.01–0.03) in both groups; the association was modified by age in adjusted analyses (P = .02), the ratio falling as age rose.
evidence.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2833888, searched in the saved page text (scratchpad/vickers_page.txt)

evidence.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph; Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors attribute the change from the crude to the adjusted estimate to people who used strips also doing things that raise overdose risk (using several drugs) and things that lower it (testing strength); they note that clients of harm-reduction sites are not representative, prior harm-reduction engagement was not measured, follow-up lasted four weeks, outcomes were self-reported, and anonymity prevented knowing why people were lost, including whether any died of overdose.
evidence.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2833888, searched in the saved page text (scratchpad/vickers_page.txt)

evidence.extracted: 120 overdoses were recorded in association with checks, 113 of them among checks made after use; the authors caution that most checks were made after use and that the decision to check may have followed an overdose. The lower crude odds of overdose with a stated intention to reduce the dose (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.18–0.89) pool checks made before and after use, have no table and cannot be read as protection (card reporting issue); there was no comparison with visits without a check.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 140 (first reader), from AI reader 137's study card

evidence.locator: Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 1st to 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Only two of the 91 articles discuss overdose-related outcomes. At a Vancouver overdose prevention site, 1% of visits included a check, mostly after use, and intended dose reduction went with lower odds of overdose (0.41) whatever the result (no intervals printed). A vending machine in Hamilton County, Ohio, dispensed 10,155 strips with naloxone and injection supplies in its first year; 105 surveyed clients reported 937 detections of fentanyl and 702 instances of discarding the drug or using less, and county overdose deaths fell by about 10% while Ohio's rose by about 5%, confounded by the naloxone from the same machine and without a control group. The review concludes that only limited data suggest strip use decreases overdose rates or overdose mortality.

evidence.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 4th paragraph; Conclusions
evidence.extracted: Among 90 studies of drug checking services to October 2019, the only one linking intentions with health outcomes was the Vancouver supervised injection site study (lower odds of overdose, OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.18–0.89, among those intending to use less), repeated without the primary study's caveats; the authors call for research linking behaviour with health outcomes and for more rigorous designs.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 140 (first reader), from AI reader 137's study card

risk_of_bias.note: Cohort: ROBINS-I serious (people chose to use strips; confounding by risk, with the crude ratio of 2.06 falling to 1.20 after adjustment; 37 in 100 of those enrolled not analysed; self-reported outcomes). The two studies relayed by the review: no comparison group, and checks that often followed the overdose.

indirectness.note: Self-reported nonfatal overdose over four weeks in people already using strips at strip-distributing services; fatal overdose not measured; North American fentanyl market.

imprecision.note: The adjusted interval (0.70 to 2.06) includes a 30% reduction and a doubling, and overdoses were rare (mean daily risk 0.02).

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; risk of bias and indirectness take one level each and imprecision two: very low. 'No detectable effect' would need an interval that excludes meaningful effects (METHODS §6.3), which this one does not, so the claim says the evidence is insufficient. Karamouzian et al.'s odds ratio of 0.41 is reported only to say why it cannot be read as an effect (card sc_karamouzian_2018, reporting issues); Karamouzian et al. is inside both reviews and is counted once. Status single study: only one study compared people who used strips with people who did not.
